extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claim limitations that recite numerical ranges — when prior art anticipates or renders obvious claimed ranges, and when amended/narrowed ranges may constitute new matter under 35 U.S.C. §112. Includes factors, case law, MPEP citations, and examiner practice notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by specific example within a claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation is considered when prior art teaches a specific example within a claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art disclosure expressly teaches a specific embodiment whose values fall within the claimed numerical range (and meets other claim limitations), that embodiment anticipates the claim (see MPEP §2131.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by prior art range entirely within claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation is considered when prior art teaches a range, or preferred range, totally within a claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art range that is wholly within the claimed range can anticipate the claim; treat range disclosures as potential species that may anticipate a genus claim (MPEP §2131.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by overlapping ranges with sufficient specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that teaches a range overlapping the claimed range anticipates if it is determined that claimed range is disclosed with sufficient specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2131.03: overlapping or touching ranges anticipate only if the prior art discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity.' Examiner must perform a fact-dependent analysis of specificity rather than mechanically equating overlap with anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species rule: species may anticipate a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a Species Anticipates a Claim to a Genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Slayter; In re Gosteli; Ex parte A) supports that a species disclosed in the prior art can anticipate a generic claim; the number of species disclosed and whether a species is preferred are immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species specifics — 'clearly envisaged' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A genus claim may be anticipated by a prior species-reference if the species would be 'at once envisage[d]' by one skilled in the art given the total circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Petering: courts consider overall circumstances (limited number of variations, substituent preferences, unchanging parent nucleus, etc.) and may treat a prior disclosure as describing each permutation 'as fully as if' each were specifically drawn or named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient specificity normally requires substantial overlap and similar function
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient specificity normally requires that there is substantial overlap in the ranges and the same or similar function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule from MPEP §2131.03: substantial overlap plus disclosure of same/similar function supports anticipation; whether this is met is fact-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for sufficient specificity analysis (size, overlap, variable nature, criticality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider in a sufficient specificity analysis: size of the ranges; extent of overlap; nature of the variables (e.g., predictable or unpredictable); criticality of claimed range relative to prior art range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to determine whether an overlapping/broad prior-art range discloses the claimed range with sufficient specificity to anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors regarding criticality of the claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the reference establishes the same or different functions/properties within the prior art range relative to the claimed range; whether data points are equivalent; whether different criteria apply at different points; and whether the prior art range is so limited the claimed species can be readily envisaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions probe whether the claimed (often narrower) range is 'critical' and thus not simply anticipated by a broader prior-art range (see MPEP §2131.03 II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient specificity is fact-dependent; narrow claims within broad references need other facts considered
rubrics_metrics.description: "What constitutes a 'sufficient specificity' is fact dependent. If the claims are directed to a narrow range, and the reference teaches a broader range, other facts of the case, must be considered."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically treat a broad prior-art range as anticipating a narrow claimed range; evaluate the totality of evidence (examples, enablement, criticality, predictability). (MPEP §2131.03 II)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results may defeat anticipation/obviousness for narrow ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art disclosure does not disclose a claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' to anticipate a claimed invention, any evidence of unexpected results within the narrow range may render the claims unobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results shown for the narrower range can rebut a prima facie case and support patentability even when a broader range exists in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires more than disclosure of a range when endpoints or specific embodiments are not disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a broad range in a reference is not the same as disclosure of each specific point or endpoint in that range; mere overlap is not always sufficient for anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atofina v. Great Lakes: a slight overlap did not disclose the claimed temperature range with sufficient specificity because the prior art disclosed only a range (not the endpoints or specific embodiment) and evidence showed the claimed range was critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encompassed prior-art ranges can support anticipation or obviousness depending on deviation and criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art range entirely encompasses a claimed narrower range, courts may find anticipation/obviousness when the encompassed range 'entirely encompasses, AND does not significantly deviate from, [the] claimed ranges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perricone/Pereira example: when the prior-art range entirely encompassed the claimed ranges and did not significantly deviate, anticipation was found; but criticality or differences can change the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness: overlapping or encompassing prior-art ranges create prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is considered when prior art teaches ranges that overlap or encompass a claimed range, or touch a claimed range at one end point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2144.05 and cases (In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff) establish that overlap/encompassment supports a prima facie obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight overlap establishes prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving overlapping ranges, even a slight overlap in range establishes a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit precedent holds that selecting a narrow range from within a somewhat broader prior-art range is prima facie obvious absent rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-overlapping but close ranges can support prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness exists where the claimed ranges and prior-art ranges do not overlap but are close enough that one skilled in the art would have expected them to have the same properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proximity of ranges would have led a person of ordinary skill to expect similar behavior across the ranges (citing In re Geisler, In re Woodruff, Titanium Metals, In re Malagari).

rubrics_metrics.name: When prior art's generic range is overly broad, selecting a narrow species may be nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference’s disclosed generic range is so broad as to encompass a very large number of possible distinct compositions, this might present a situation analogous to the nonobviousness of a claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very broad genus in the prior art may not render every narrow species obvious — consider the number of distinct compositions and whether the species would have been 'clearly envisaged.' (See In re Peterson discussion and related cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebutting a prima facie case of obviousness for ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness based on ranges by showing the criticality of the claimed range, that the art teaches away, or by presenting evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §716.02–§716.02(g) and cases In re Geisler; provide evidence of criticality (comparative data, unexpected properties) or teaching-away to overcome prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations must be considered but do not necessarily control
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence pertaining to secondary considerations must be taken into account whenever present; however, it does not necessarily control the obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider objective indicia (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, etc.) as part of the obviousness analysis, but weigh them with other evidence (Pfizer v. Apotex; Leapfrog; Newell Cos.; Cubist Pharm.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 102/103 combination rejection when specificity unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. §§102/103 combination rejection is permitted if it is unclear if the reference teaches the range with 'sufficient specificity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a combined rejection, the examiner must provide reasons for anticipation and also a reasoned statement regarding obviousness (MPEP §2131.03 II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph guidance for making 102/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph example: 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: This form paragraph is NOT intended to be commonly used as a substitute for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. A single rejection under either 102 or 103 should be made whenever possible using appropriate form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description/new matter standard for ranges (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for written description compliance is whether the disclosure of the application as originally filed reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance is a question of fact determined case-by-case; the required level of detail varies with the nature/scope of the claims and the complexity/predictability of the technology (Vas-Cath; Ariad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining whether original disclosure conveys a later-claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider (1) explicit/implicit disclosure of a generic range encompassing the new range; (2) specific/preferred/exemplified embodiments relating to the new range; (3) explicit/implicit disclosure that particular ranges are part of the inventor's invention; (4) disclosure of direction/guidance for obtaining ranges; (5) complexity/unpredictability of the invention; (6) evidence that the new range is a different invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to assess whether an amendment to add or narrow a range adds new matter under §112(a). Presence of examples, preferred embodiments, or explicit guidance supports written-description sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal endpoint support not always required for new endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal support for a newly claimed endpoint is not required; the original disclosure may still reasonably convey possession of the later-claimed endpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte Jackson and In re Wertheim — specific examples at certain values may support a broader (or shifted) claimed range if persons skilled in the art would regard the claimed range as part of the invention; do not let form triumph over substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner approach to §112(a) rejections with amended ranges (practical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant narrows a claim to a sub-range and presents evidence of unexpected results unique to that sub-range, do not necessarily maintain a §103 rejection; instead, consider making a §112(a) new matter rejection if the narrower range lacks written-description support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides' examples: (1) amendment without literal support to 62.5-100 ppm — likely no §112(a) rejection absent reason to doubt that the broader disclosure describes the narrower range; (2) amendment to 40-50 ppm with a declaration of unexpected results — drop the §103 rejection (prima facie case overcome) and make a §112(a) rejection because applicant is asserting the narrower range is a different invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitation is a genus limitation; prior-art embodiments within claimed range will anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A range limitation is a genus limitation. Embodiments disclosed in the prior art that fall within the claimed range (and meet all other claim limitations) will anticipate the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only ranges are disclosed in the prior art, the disclosed ranges must be considered to determine whether they anticipate the claimed range; overlapping ranges also raise obviousness issues; evidence of criticality impacts both anticipation and obviousness.
